title: Hirschsprung Disease
subject: Surgery
summary: A congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells causing functional obstruction of the distal colon. Presents early with failure to pass meconium and abdominal distension, requiring prompt diagnosis and surgical resection.

sections.p: Hirschsprung disease (HD) is a congenital aganglionosis of the submucosal and myenteric plexuses, usually involving the rectum and extending proximally. Diagnosis is confirmed by rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells and a positive acetylcholinesterase stain.

t.b: Detects absence of ganglion cells; a positive result confirms HD.
Highlights increased enzyme activity in aganglionic segments; a positive stain supports diagnosis.
Shows dilated colon with transition zone; a sudden change in caliber suggests HD.
Defines transition zone and rule out other causes of obstruction.
Failure to pass meconium within 48–72 h is a key clinical clue.

sections.p: Severity is staged by the length of aganglionic segment and presence of enterocolitis. The Krickenbeck classification (distal, long segment, total colonic) guides surgical planning.
b: Long segment – extends into sigmoid/descending colon

sections.p: The primary cause is a failure of neural crest cell migration during embryogenesis. Genetic mutations (RET, EDNRB, EDN3) and chromosomal anomalies (trisomy 21) are common.

t.b: Detects trisomy 21 or other chromosomal abnormalities associated with HD.
Identifies familial risk and guides genetic counseling.

sections.p: Neonates present with failure to pass meconium, abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and sometimes bilious stool. Older children may have chronic constipation, abdominal pain, and failure to thrive.

t.b: Empty rectum on digital rectal exam; a gush of stool on withdrawal is classic.
Delayed weight gain indicates chronic obstruction.

sections.p: Investigations focus on confirming aganglionosis and ruling out other causes of obstruction. In low‑resource settings, a plain X‑ray and contrast enema are often the first steps.

t.b: Shows dilated colon with transition zone; absence of gas in rectum suggests obstruction.
Defines transition zone; a sudden change in caliber supports HD.
Gold standard; absence of ganglion cells confirms diagnosis.
Positive in aganglionic segments; used when biopsy is equivocal.

sections.p: Enterocolitis, perforation, electrolyte imbalance, and sepsis are life‑threatening complications. Early recognition and treatment are essential.
b: Enterocolitis – fever, abdominal pain, bloody stool

t.b: Suggests enterocolitis; requires urgent antibiotics and bowel rest.
May indicate perforation; look for free air on X‑ray.
Hyponatremia, hypokalemia common; correct before surgery.

sections.p: Initial management includes bowel rest, nasogastric suction, and broad‑spectrum antibiotics for enterocolitis. Definitive treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with pull‑through anastomosis.

t.b: Treat enterocolitis; avoid metronidazole if renal impairment.
Resects aganglionic segment; options include Duhamel, Soave, or Swenson techniques.

sections.p: Post‑operative care includes monitoring for anastomotic leak, constipation, and enterocolitis. Long‑term follow‑up focuses on bowel function and growth.

t.b: Normalizes to 1–3 stools/day; fewer stools suggest obstruction.
Weight and height should catch up within 6–12 months post‑surgery.

sections.p: Functional constipation, colonic atresia, and meconium ileus can mimic HD. Distinguishing features include the transition zone on imaging and biopsy findings.

t.b: Absence of transition zone suggests functional constipation.
Presence of ganglion cells rules out HD.

sections.p: A normal X‑ray may occur in early disease; a negative biopsy can be due to sampling error. Clinical correlation is essential.

t.b: Superficial samples may miss ganglion cells; ensure full thickness.

whenToSeekHelp: Abdominal perforation signs (free air on X‑ray)

faq.q: Why is Hirschsprung disease more common in males?
faq.a: The exact reason is unclear, but genetic and hormonal factors may influence neural crest migration differently in males.

faq.q: Can Hirschsprung disease be diagnosed after the first year of life?
faq.a: Yes, especially in short‑segment disease; chronic constipation and abdominal distension may prompt investigation later.

faq.q: What is the role of the RET gene in Hirschsprung disease?
faq.a: RET mutations impair neural crest cell migration, leading to aganglionosis; they are found in about 30% of familial cases.

exam: What is the most specific test to confirm Hirschsprung disease? — Rectal suction biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells and positive acetylcholinesterase stain.
Which complication requires immediate surgical intervention? — Perforation with free air on abdominal X‑ray.
Why is metronidazole avoided in patients with renal impairment? — It is renally excreted and can accumulate, causing toxicity.
What is the first step in managing a neonate with suspected Hirschsprung disease? — Bowel rest, NG suction, and broad‑spectrum antibiotics for enterocolitis.
How does a contrast enema help differentiate Hirschsprung disease from functional constipation? — It shows a transition zone in HD, absent in functional constipation.
What is the most common associated chromosomal abnormality in Hirschsprung disease? — Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).
